summary:
At the Moon's south pole the Sun never rises more than a few degrees, so a single ridge decides whether a lander has power and a radio link to Earth. Claude's P.L.A.N answers, for any site and any hour from 2026 to 2029, whether the Sun and Earth are above the real terrain skyline, using NASA's LRO LOLA elevation data and JPL's DE421 ephemeris, and checked against JPL Horizons (0.0007 degrees) and NASA's own illumination maps (within 4.3 points).

The web app has a Simple view for anyone and a Detailed view for mission planners. It compares landing sites, shows what a two-week launch slip costs, finds every day a mission can land, and tests the whole polar region against NASA's Artemis III landing requirements: 14.3% of the ground passes, in 5,297 "Goldilocks zones". A VR mode on Meta Quest 3, with a narrated three-stage journey, lets you fly to the pole and stand at a landing site as the real Sun and Earth move across its sky.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Claude's P.L.A.N (Polar Lunar Augmented Navigation) answers the two questions a south-pole lander lives or dies by: will it have sunlight for power, and will it see Earth for a direct radio link? One website, two views: Simple (plain steps: "Explore a site", "Plan a landing") and Detailed (every tool), both using the same data and scoring.

- Overview: pick a site and a date; the whole horizon is unrolled with the real skyline, the Sun's path and Earth's wobble, and one sentence says what it means for a lander.

- Compare sites and slip the launch: at Nobile Rim 1 a 10-day stay starting 9 January 2027 has 100% sunlight; land 14 days later and it has 12.5%.

- Window Finder: describe the mission, get every landing day that works. A 14-day mission at Malapert Massif can land on 32 of the next 365 days.

- Site Finder (landing map): every 120 m square within 6 degrees of the pole is tested against NASA's Artemis III landing requirements. 14.3% of the ground passes all of them, in 5,297 "Goldilocks zones". Green / amber / red per criterion; ground that fails a NASA limit is hatched and says which limit. Click any spot for its numbers, strengths, weaknesses and how sure we are.

- VR (Meta Quest 3, in the browser): a three-stage journey (the whole Moon, the south pole, standing on the surface) with the real Sun and Earth moving over the real skyline, an AI voice narrator that explains what you see, sound effects, teleporting, and a movable menu.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline computes the Sun and Earth as seen from the Moon every hour (Skyfield, JPL DE421), and for each site the terrain skyline: from NASA's LOLA elevation map we look outward in 720 directions up to 150 km, allowing for the Moon's curvature. The browser combines both: the Sun or Earth is "up" when its centre is above the skyline. Everything runs in the browser from static files.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS RIGHT

Sun and Earth positions differ from JPL Horizons by at most 0.0007 degrees. Long-run sunlight differs from NASA Goddard's PGDA illumination maps by at most 3.5 percentage points and Earth visibility by at most 4.3, over the nine Artemis candidate sites. 57 Python tests, 166 browser maths tests and end-to-end browser tests run on every change.

WHAT WE FOUND

- Sunlight, Earth visibility and slope each rule out about half of the polar region; together they leave 14.3%.

- A few hundred metres matter: near Malapert Massif, sunlight ranges from 0% to 56% within 2.5 km.

- Which region is best depends on the mission: Malapert Massif ranks 1st for the radio link (Earth always in view).

- Honest limit: the spot where the IM-2 lander came down in 2025 passes our limits on a 120 m map, but it fell into a crater 20 m across. Passing means "worth a closer look with finer data", not "safe to land".

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Mission planners, students and the public can see in seconds what otherwise takes an illumination study: which sites work, when, and why, in plain words, on a phone or in VR, shareable as a link that reopens the exact view. All intermediate results are published so others can check and build on them.

TOOLS

Python (Skyfield, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, pytest), TypeScript, React, Vite, d3, zustand, vitest, Playwright, Meta's Immersive Web SDK with three.js for VR, GitHub Actions, Vercel, a Meta Quest 3, ElevenLabs for the narrator voice. Code: https://github.com/eugeniobusta/lunar-navigator

This is not an official NASA product and implies no NASA endorsement.
